reading.title: Peace by Talking
reading.purpose: Compare two real settlements to see how outside helpers can end a bitter dispute.
paras: Conflicts rarely end the moment someone wins an argument. More often they end because someone finds a way to break the cycle. History offers two famous examples of nations choosing words over weapons, and both show how a dispute can escalate, stall, and finally calm down.

In 1904, Russia and Japan went to war over land and influence in northeast Asia. After more than a year of fighting, both sides were worn out, but each remained a hostile adversary, an opponent who distrusted the other. Every offer seemed like a trick, and neither government wanted to look weak. President Theodore Roosevelt offered to mediate, which meant helping both sides talk and suggesting ways to settle. In August 1905 he brought delegates to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and the talks soon reached an impasse over money and land.

Roosevelt did not order either side to give in. Instead he kept both delegations talking. Japan finally dropped its demand for money, and Russia agreed to give up part of an island. The treaty was signed in September 1905, and Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize the next year for his role.

A different kind of settlement came in 1872. During the American Civil War, warships built in Britain had raided American merchant ships, and the United States demanded payment. Each government could have chosen to retaliate with threats or trade limits. Instead they agreed to arbitrate, which means letting a neutral panel decide and promising to accept the decision. The panel met in Geneva, Switzerland, heard both sides, and ordered Britain to pay the United States 15.5 million dollars. Both nations accepted the ruling.

These cases show a pattern that applies even to schoolyard quarrels. A calm third party can defuse a standoff, but defusing is not the same as giving in. To appease a side is to calm it by giving in to what it wants, and that differs from helping both sides find a fair deal. Both settlements also took time and patience. In the second case, the United States and Britain were able to reconcile, and they later settled other disputes in similar ways.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "arbitrate" most nearly means
choices: to let a neutral panel decide a dispute and accept its decision
to strike back at an opponent who has caused you harm or insulted you
to stay silent in a meeting until the other side finally gives in completely
to move a dispute to a much larger and more crowded court of law
qs.why: The sentence explains it: arbitrating means "letting a neutral panel decide and promising to accept the decision."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how the talks at Portsmouth moved past the impasse?
choices: Roosevelt did not order either side to give in.
Instead he kept both delegations talking.
Japan finally dropped its demand for money, and Russia agreed to give up part of an island.
The treaty was signed in September 1905, and Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize the next year for his role.
qs.why: This is the sentence where each side gives up something, which is how the talks finally ended.

ev.text: Japan finally dropped its demand for money, and Russia agreed to give up part of an island.

qs.q: Why was a neutral helper useful to Russia and Japan in 1905?
choices: Each government believed that a helper from outside would take its side against the other.
Neither side trusted the other's offers, but both could listen to an outsider.
The two governments had never before met in the same room to discuss the war.
Only an American president has the power to end a war between two other nations.
qs.why: The text says every offer seemed like a trick to the other side, so a trusted outsider could keep the talks going.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Disputes end only when one side is completely defeated by the other side in a long fight.
A country should give in quickly whenever another country makes a demand of any kind.
Disputes can end through patient talks with a neutral helper instead of through force.
Presidents are always better than judges at settling quarrels between large nations.
qs.why: Both examples show a bitter dispute settled by a neutral helper, and the last paragraph says that this approach takes time and patience.

clues.text: helping both sides talk and suggesting ways to settle
an opponent who distrusted the other
letting a neutral panel decide and promising to accept the decision
calm it by giving in to what it wants

needsReview.reason: Facts about the 1905 Portsmouth talks (war began 1904, talks in Portsmouth, New Hampshire in August 1905, 'money and land' as the impasse); well documented but a person should check wording.
Treaty signed September 1905 and Roosevelt's Nobel Peace Prize in 1906; Russia ceded 'part of an island' (southern Sakhalin) and Japan dropped its indemnity demand.
Alabama Claims arbitration: Geneva tribunal, 1872, Britain ordered to pay 15.5 million dollars; confirm wording about 'warships built in Britain' (Confederate raiders).
